case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 8 U.S.C. § 1252(d)(1) is a jurisdictional bar or instead a waivable/forfeitable claims-processing rule, and whether it requires a noncitizen to file a discretionary motion to reconsider with the BIA to exhaust administrative remedies before seeking judicial review.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(d)(1) (requiring exhaustion of “all administrative remedies available to the alien as of right” before judicial review of a final order of removal).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that § 1252(d)(1) is not jurisdictional under the Supreme Court’s modern ‘clear statement’ approach; it is at most a mandatory claims-processing rule that can be waived or forfeited by the government. Petitioner also contends that exhaustion of remedies ‘available … as of right’ does not include filing a motion to reconsider, because reconsideration is discretionary (not an entitlement) and cannot be required as a prerequisite to judicial review—especially when the alleged error is the BIA’s own impermissible factfinding, which arises from the BIA decision itself.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondent argues the Fifth Circuit correctly refused to review petitioner’s impermissible-factfinding claim because petitioner did not exhaust it by filing a motion to reconsider with the BIA. The government’s position, as framed in the question presented, is that § 1252(d)(1) prevented review where the noncitizen failed to give the agency the first opportunity to correct its own error via reconsideration, and that the exhaustion requirement operates as a threshold limitation on the court of appeals’ ability to entertain the claim.

Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner, 142 S. Ct. 1493 (2022)
Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Henderson ex rel. Henderson v. Shinseki, 562 U.S. 428 (2011)
Reed Elsevier, Inc. v. Muchnick, 559 U.S. 154 (2010)

Union Pacific R. Co. v. Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, 558 U.S. 67 (2009)
United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 140 S. Ct. 1575 (2020)
Gill v. INS, 420 F.3d 82 (2d Cir. 2005) (as referenced regarding exhaustion in circuits)
Ramirez v. Sessions, 887 F.3d 693 (4th Cir. 2018) (as referenced regarding exhaustion in circuits)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s functional argument—that reconsideration best serves exhaustion by giving the BIA a chance to correct its own errors—has force in an overburdened system, but it cannot overcome the statutory limitation to remedies “available … as of right.” As Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan emphasize under Arbaugh/Fort Bend/Boechler, we do not treat such threshold requirements as jurisdictional absent a clear statement, and the INA’s nearby use of expressly jurisdictional language makes the contrast especially telling. Union Pacific, invoked by Justice Thomas, reinforces my view that exhaustion-type rules are typically claims-processing unless Congress unmistakably provides otherwise; it does not authorize us to expand “as of right” to include discretionary reconsideration. A narrow disposition remains available: hold § 1252(d)(1) nonjurisdictional and not requiring reconsideration when the asserted error originates in the BIA’s own decision, without opining broadly on other issue-exhaustion scenarios.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Alito’s functional point—that reconsideration gives the BIA an additional opportunity to correct its own errors—does not overcome the statutory text limiting exhaustion to remedies “available … as of right.” As Justice Barrett and the Chief Justice emphasize, a motion to reconsider is discretionary in outcome and thus not an “as of right” remedy in the ordinary public meaning of that phrase; reading it in would effectively erase Congress’s limiting words. On the jurisdictional label, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Arbaugh/Fort Bend/Boechler’s clear-statement rule, reinforced by the INA’s adjacent, expressly jurisdictional provisions—textual contrast cuts strongly against treating § 1252(d)(1) as jurisdictional. Union Pacific supports enforcing exhaustion principles where Congress has imposed them, but it cannot justify expanding the statutory exhaustion requirement beyond its enacted terms.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett are right to stress Arbaugh/Fort Bend/Boechler’s clear-statement discipline on the jurisdictional label, and I can accept § 1252(d)(1) as claims-processing without yielding the case. But their textual point about “as of right” is weaker than they suggest: the relevant “remedy” is the noncitizen’s entitlement to invoke reconsideration on specified grounds within the time limit—not an entitlement to win—so it is “available … as of right” in the ordinary sense that one may file it and obtain agency consideration. Union Pacific, which Justice Thomas invokes, reinforces the core purpose of exhaustion to give the agency a fair opportunity to correct its own legal errors before judicial review; in immigration that purpose has concrete enforcement and delay consequences that Congress reasonably would have wanted to avoid. Treating reconsideration as optional when the alleged error is the BIA’s own decision invites immediate judicial intervention in precisely the circumstance where the agency can most efficiently self-correct, and I do not think the “as of right” phrase compels that result.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point—that reconsideration gives the BIA a fair opportunity to correct its own legal errors—has force as a matter of administrative design, but it cannot overcome Congress’s limiting phrase “remedies available … as of right.” As Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch stress, a motion to reconsider is discretionary in outcome and thus not naturally “as of right,” and reading it in effectively writes those words out, creating a procedural snare for often-unrepresented noncitizens with little added agency-primacy benefit when the claimed error is already in the BIA’s decision. On the jurisdictional label, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Arbaugh/Fort Bend/Boechler’s clear-statement rule is dispositive given the INA’s nearby explicit jurisdictional language—so § 1252(d)(1) is best treated as nonjurisdictional and, on the merits, does not mandate reconsideration here. Union Pacific, as Justice Thomas notes, supports respecting exhaustion’s purposes, but it also reinforces that we shouldn’t convert such requirements into jurisdictional or expand them beyond the statutory text.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—the agency should get a prompt chance to fix its own errors—has real force as a matter of administration, but it cannot overcome Congress’s limiting words: § 1252(d)(1) requires exhaustion only of remedies “available … as of right,” and a motion to reconsider is discretionary in outcome and thus not naturally within that phrase. As the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett stress, our clear-statement cases (Arbaugh, Fort Bend, Boechler) require unmistakable jurisdictional language, and the INA’s nearby use of expressly jurisdictional terms makes the absence here especially telling; function alone cannot supply what the text withholds. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Union Pacific does not push the other way for me: it supports treating exhaustion/channeling rules as claims-processing absent a clear jurisdictional hook, and it does not authorize reading “as of right” to include discretionary reconsideration. Given that the alleged error arises in the BIA’s own decision, forcing reconsideration as a mandatory precondition risks creating a non-textual procedural trap without the clear congressional instruction our cases demand.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s functional point—that reconsideration best serves exhaustion by giving the BIA a prompt chance to fix its own mistakes—has real force, but it cannot overcome the enacted limitation that exhaustion reaches only remedies “available … as of right.” As Justice Barrett stresses, a motion to reconsider is discretionary in outcome and thus not an “as of right” remedy in the ordinary legal sense; treating it as mandatory would effectively read those limiting words out of § 1252(d)(1). On the jurisdictional question, I remain with the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan that Arbaugh/Fort Bend/Boechler’s clear-statement rule governs: Congress knew how to speak in jurisdictional terms elsewhere in the INA and did not do so here, and Union Pacific (as Justice Thomas notes) supports treating exhaustion-like rules as nonjurisdictional absent a clear congressional directive. I therefore see no textual or precedential basis to re-label (d)(1) as jurisdictional or to expand it to require discretionary reconsideration.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point—that reconsideration serves exhaustion’s core purpose by giving the BIA a prompt chance to fix its own mistakes—has real practical force in a high-volume system, and I take seriously his Union Pacific channeling concern. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, our Arbaugh/Fort Bend/Boechler clear-statement framework does not allow functional considerations to turn § 1252(d)(1) into a jurisdictional bar absent unmistakable jurisdictional language, especially when nearby INA provisions use express jurisdictional terms. On the merits of what must be exhausted, Alito’s reading treats a discretionary motion to reconsider as a remedy “available … as of right,” which (as Justice Gorsuch notes) effectively erases Congress’s limiting words; the right to file a motion is not the same as a right to have the agency entertain or grant it. Institutionally, maintaining the jurisdiction/claims-processing distinction preserves clarity and legitimacy while still allowing enforcement through waiver/forfeiture and ordinary issue-exhaustion rules where appropriate.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is functional: reconsideration lets the BIA correct its own errors promptly and thus serves the core purpose of exhaustion. But § 1252(d)(1) does not ask what is most efficient; it requires exhaustion only of remedies “available … as of right,” and a motion to reconsider is not something the alien is entitled to obtain—so reading it in would dilute Congress’s limiting words, as Justice Thomas emphasizes. On the jurisdictional question, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that, under Arbaugh/Fort Bend/Boechler’s clear-statement rule, § 1252(d)(1) lacks the jurisdictional vocabulary Congress typically uses when withdrawing adjudicatory power, especially in a statute that elsewhere speaks in expressly jurisdictional terms. Alito’s reliance on Union Pacific underscores why courts may enforce issue-exhaustion principles, but it does not supply the clear textual hook needed either to make § 1252(d)(1) jurisdictional or to convert discretionary reconsideration into an “as of right” remedy.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s functional argument—that reconsideration gives the BIA a quick opportunity to correct its own errors and avoids fragmented review—has force, especially in a high-volume system. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 1252(d)(1) limits exhaustion to remedies “available … as of right,” and a motion to reconsider is discretionary in the only sense that matters for procedural fairness: the noncitizen has no entitlement to obtain reconsideration, so making it mandatory would turn Congress’s limiting phrase into a trapdoor. On the jurisdictional label, the Arbaugh/Fort Bend/Boechler clear-statement framework (invoked by Roberts, Kagan, and Barrett) and the INA’s contrastive use of explicit jurisdictional language elsewhere undercut treating (d)(1) as jurisdiction-stripping, which also aligns with Union Pacific’s caution against converting exhaustion rules into nonwaivable bars absent clear direction. I therefore maintain that courts can enforce exhaustion as a claims-processing rule without rewriting “as of right” to require discretionary reconsideration, particularly where the asserted defect originates in the BIA’s own decision.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under this Court’s clear-statement approach, § 1252(d)(1)’s exhaustion requirement is best read as a mandatory claims-processing rule, not a jurisdictional bar, because Congress did not “clearly state” it limits the court’s adjudicatory power. See Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp. and Fort Bend County v. Davis; treating it as jurisdictional would also disrupt ordinary party presentation and risk unfair prejudice. On the merits of what must be exhausted, the text requires only those remedies “available … as of right,” and a motion to reconsider before the BIA is discretionary, so it is not a prerequisite to judicial review of a claim that arises from the BIA’s own decision. This narrow construction preserves agency primacy where Congress demanded it, while avoiding an extra, non-textual exhaustion step that would unnecessarily burden review in a high-volume system.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of § 1252(d)(1) requires exhaustion only of remedies “available to the alien as of right,” which excludes a discretionary motion to reconsider before the BIA; Congress’s words foreclose reading an additional mandatory reconsideration step into the statute. Nor does § 1252(d)(1) clearly speak in jurisdictional terms, and under this Court’s clear-statement approach a precondition to relief is not treated as jurisdictional absent unmistakable language, see Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006), and Henderson ex rel. Henderson v. Shinseki, 562 U.S. 428 (2011). Union Pacific R. Co. v. Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, 558 U.S. 67 (2009), likewise treats exhaustion-type requirements as nonjurisdictional claims-processing rules unless Congress clearly provides otherwise. Because petitioner’s claim arose from asserted BIA error in its own decision, requiring a discretionary reconsideration motion would contradict the statute’s “as of right” limitation and improperly expand the exhaustion obligation beyond the enacted text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1252(d)(1) conditions judicial review on the noncitizen having exhausted “all administrative remedies available to the alien as of right,” and that text is best read to require use of the agency’s established reconsideration mechanism when the alleged error is the BIA’s own and can be corrected promptly by the Board itself. Even if modern “clear statement” cases (e.g., Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp. and Henderson v. Shinseki) counsel caution before labeling rules jurisdictional, the practical function of § 1252(d)(1) is a firm threshold limitation in immigration review designed to keep courts from addressing issues the agency has not had a fair opportunity to fix. Union Pacific R. Co. v. Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers underscores the importance of respecting exhaustion doctrines that channel disputes back to the agency and prevent premature judicial intervention, which is especially significant in removal cases where delay and fragmentation have concrete enforcement consequences. Because petitioner bypassed reconsideration and thereby denied the BIA a first chance to correct its own alleged impermissible factfinding, the court of appeals properly declined review under § 1252(d)(1).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1252(d)(1) is best read as a nonjurisdictional claims-processing rule because Congress did not “clearly state” it limits jurisdiction, especially compared to nearby INA provisions that expressly speak in jurisdictional terms; under Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner and Arbaugh, that absence is decisive. The statutory text requires exhaustion only of remedies “available to the alien as of right,” and a motion to reconsider is discretionary, so it cannot be demanded as a prerequisite to judicial review—particularly where the asserted error (impermissible BIA factfinding) arises from the BIA’s own decision. Treating (d)(1) as jurisdictional and requiring discretionary reconsideration would create procedural traps that disproportionately block review for vulnerable noncitizens and undermine fairness and access to justice. Because the rule is nonjurisdictional, the government may waive or forfeit it, consistent with Fort Bend County v. Davis and the Court’s broader clear-statement jurisprudence.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 1252(d)(1) lacks the clear jurisdictional statement this Court now requires, so it is best read as a mandatory claims-processing rule subject to waiver and forfeiture rather than a limit on the court of appeals’ power. Under Boechler, Arbaugh, and Fort Bend County, Congress must speak clearly when it seeks to make a precondition to review jurisdictional, and the INA elsewhere uses expressly jurisdictional language—suggesting § 1252(d)(1) is not. On the merits of exhaustion, the text requires exhaustion of remedies “available … as of right,” which does not naturally include a discretionary motion to reconsider; requiring reconsideration would also be unworkable where the alleged error arises from the BIA’s own decision. The court may still enforce issue exhaustion as a prudential or regulatory matter, but § 1252(d)(1) itself should not be stretched to compel discretionary reconsideration as a prerequisite to judicial review.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 1252(d)(1) lacks the requisite clear statement that it strips courts of adjudicatory power, so under Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp. and Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner it is best read as a mandatory claims-processing rule subject to waiver and forfeiture, not a jurisdictional bar. The text requires exhaustion only of remedies “available … as of right,” which does not naturally include a discretionary motion to reconsider before the BIA; reading “as of right” to cover discretionary reconsideration would erase Congress’s limiting words. Requiring reconsideration here would also impose an extra-statutory trap for issue exhaustion when the alleged error arises from the BIA’s own decision, contrary to the provision’s plain meaning and the Court’s insistence on disciplined use of “jurisdiction.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under this Court’s clear-statement framework, § 1252(d)(1) is not jurisdictional because Congress did not clearly state that the exhaustion requirement limits the courts’ subject-matter power; it is therefore a mandatory but waivable/forfeitable claims-processing rule. See Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006); Fort Bend County v. Davis, 139 S. Ct. 1843 (2019); Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner, 142 S. Ct. 1493 (2022). And the statutory text requires exhaustion only of remedies “available to the alien as of right,” which does not naturally encompass a discretionary motion to reconsider before the BIA. Reading the statute to compel a discretionary reconsideration motion would add an extra procedural hurdle not grounded in the text and would be impractical and unworkable where the alleged error arises from the BIA’s own decision itself.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under the Court’s clear-statement rule, § 1252(d)(1) is best read as a mandatory claims-processing rule, not a jurisdictional bar, because it lacks the kind of jurisdictional language Congress uses when it truly withdraws adjudicatory power. See Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp. and Fort Bend County v. Davis (treating exhaustion-like requirements as nonjurisdictional absent a clear statement), reinforced by Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner (requiring a clear statement for jurisdictional limits). Textually, the phrase “administrative remedies available to the alien as of right” does not encompass a discretionary motion to reconsider before the BIA, which the Board may deny in its discretion; requiring such a motion would read “as of right” out of the statute. Because the government can waive or forfeit nonjurisdictional exhaustion objections, the court of appeals should not have treated the omission of a reconsideration motion as a jurisdictional defect.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 1252(d)(1) lacks the clear jurisdictional language Congress typically uses, so under this Court’s clear-statement framework it is best read as a mandatory but waivable/forfeitable claims-processing rule rather than a jurisdictional bar. See Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner, 142 S. Ct. 1493 (2022), and Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006). On the exhaustion question, the statute requires only those remedies “available ... as of right,” 8 U.S.C. § 1252(d)(1), which does not naturally include a discretionary motion to reconsider—especially when the alleged error (impermissible factfinding) arises from the BIA’s own decision and reconsideration is not an entitlement. Treating reconsideration as mandatory would create unfair procedural traps and unnecessarily foreclose judicial review in a context with severe liberty consequences, contrary to the pragmatic and fairness-focused approach reflected in Henderson v. Shinseki, 562 U.S. 428 (2011).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 8 U.S.C. § 1252(d)(1) makes issue exhaustion a jurisdictional bar to judicial review—and specifically whether a noncitizen must file a discretionary motion to reconsider with the BIA to satisfy exhaustion before raising a claim in the court of appeals.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(d)(1) (requiring a noncitizen to exhaust “all administrative remedies available to the alien as of right” before seeking judicial review).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The petitioner argues that § 1252(d)(1) is not jurisdictional under the Supreme Court’s modern “clear statement” approach; instead it is a mandatory claims-processing rule that can be waived or forfeited by the government. The petitioner also contends that filing a motion to reconsider is not an “administrative remed[y] available ... as of right” because reconsideration is discretionary with the BIA, so failure to move for reconsideration cannot be treated as failure to exhaust. Relatedly, petitioner maintains that requiring reconsideration to preserve issues would impose severe, unfair, and impractical burdens in high-volume immigration adjudication, contrary to ordinary adversarial principles and the Court’s recent efforts to cabin overuse of the jurisdictional label.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The respondent (United States) argues that the Fifth Circuit correctly refused to review petitioner’s claim (that the BIA engaged in impermissible factfinding) because petitioner did not first present that claim to the agency through a motion to reconsider. In the government’s view, § 1252(d)(1) precludes court-of-appeals review of issues not properly exhausted before the BIA; a motion to reconsider is the proper administrative mechanism to give the Board the first opportunity to correct alleged legal error, including claims that the BIA exceeded its role by factfinding, and therefore the exhaustion requirement blocks judicial review when such a motion was not filed.

Boechler, P.C. v. Commissioner, 142 S. Ct. 1493 (2022)
Henderson v. Shinseki, 562 U.S. 428 (2011)
Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Reed Elsevier, Inc. v. Muchnick, 559 U.S. 154 (2010)
United States v. Kwai Fun Wong, 575 U.S. 402 (2015)
Union Pacific R. Co. v. Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, 558 U.S. 67 (2009)
United States v. Sineneng-Smith, 140 S. Ct. 1575 (2020)
Ramirez v. Sessions, 887 F.3d 693 (4th Cir. 2018)
Gill v. INS, 420 F.3d 82 (2d Cir. 2005)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s functional point—that reconsideration lets the BIA correct legal errors before judicial review—remains the best argument for the other side, but it cannot overcome Congress’s textual limit to remedies “available … as of right.” As Justice Thomas and Justice Kagan emphasize, 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a) makes reconsideration discretionary, and reading “as of right” to mean only a right to file would drain that limiting phrase of independent meaning. On the jurisdictional label, the clear-statement line (Arbaugh, Henderson, Boechler) that Justice Barrett and Justice Sotomayor invoke reinforces my view that § 1252(d)(1) is a mandatory claims-processing rule, not a power-stripping bar, consistent with Union Pacific’s distinction between mandatory procedure and jurisdiction. A narrow holding—nonjurisdictional and no categorical requirement to pursue discretionary reconsideration—corrects the Fifth Circuit without unsettling ordinary issue-exhaustion where the agency provides a genuine avenue of relief as of right.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest argument—pressed most in Justice Alito’s functional account—is that reconsideration best serves exhaustion by letting the BIA correct legal error first, but text controls: § 1252(d)(1) requires exhaustion only of remedies “available … as of right,” and 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a) makes reconsideration discretionary, not an entitlement. As the Chief Justice notes, redefining “as of right” to mean merely a right-to-file collapses the limiting phrase and effectively adds an extra step Congress did not impose. The clear-statement line Justice Kagan and others invoke (Arbaugh, Henderson, Boechler, Fort Bend) confirms we should not transform this into a jurisdictional bar absent unmistakable jurisdictional language, and Union Pacific—emphasized by Justice Gorsuch—reinforces keeping discretionary agency processes from becoming judge-made jurisdictional gatekeepers. Therefore the Fifth Circuit’s categorical, jurisdictional reconsideration requirement cannot be squared with the statute’s original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Respondent’s strongest point is functional: requiring reconsideration better serves exhaustion by giving the BIA a final chance to correct legal errors and promotes administrative efficiency. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 1252(d)(1) exhausts only remedies “available … as of right,” and 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a) makes reconsideration discretionary, so a categorical requirement would rewrite the statute by collapsing “as of right” into a mere permission to file. Roberts’s and Kagan’s reliance on Arbaugh/Henderson/Boechler also matters: absent a clear statement, we should not treat § 1252(d)(1) as jurisdictional, and Union Pacific supports enforcing exhaustion rules as written rather than adding judge-made hurdles. The government remains free to argue ordinary issue exhaustion/forfeiture when an argument was not fairly presented to the agency, but it cannot convert a discretionary reconsideration motion into a mandatory gateway to review.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest point—Justice Alito’s functional argument that reconsideration best serves exhaustion by letting the BIA correct its own legal errors—cannot overcome Congress’s textual limit to remedies “available … as of right.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a) makes reconsideration discretionary, and treating a discretionary request as mandatory collapses the “as of right” constraint into a mere right-to-file, effectively rewriting the statute. On jurisdiction, the clear-statement line Roberts cites (Arbaugh, Henderson, Boechler) and Union Pacific reinforce that even sensible process rules should remain nonjurisdictional, avoiding sua sponte forfeiture policing that predictably harms unrepresented noncitizens. The government retains ordinary issue-exhaustion/forfeiture tools, but it cannot convert discretionary reconsideration into a categorical prerequisite to judicial review.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The opposing-side’s strongest point remains the functional exhaustion argument: a motion to reconsider gives the BIA a chance to correct its own legal error before judicial review. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 1252(d)(1) exhausts only remedies “available … as of right,” and 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a) makes reconsideration discretionary—so making it mandatory would drain the limiting phrase of meaning and effectively rewrite the statute. Justice Sotomayor’s practical concern reinforces the clear-statement cases (Arbaugh, Henderson, Boechler, Fort Bend): absent unmistakable jurisdictional language, we should not transform a sensible procedural norm into a jurisdictional bar that courts must raise sua sponte. Union Pacific supports the same boundary—mandatory claims-processing rules can be enforced when invoked, but we should not elevate discretionary agency mechanisms into categorical, power-stripping prerequisites.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The strongest opposing argument—Justice Alito’s functional point that reconsideration best serves exhaustion by letting the BIA correct error—cannot overcome Congress’s textual limitation to remedies “available … as of right.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a) makes reconsideration discretionary, so treating it as mandatory would read “as of right” to mean only “permitted to file,” collapsing the limiting phrase and effectively adding a judicially invented prerequisite. On the jurisdictional label, the clear-statement line (Arbaugh, Henderson, Boechler, Fort Bend), which several colleagues cite, reinforces that § 1252(d)(1) is at most a mandatory claims-processing rule—consistent with Union Pacific’s distinction between process prescriptions and true power-stripping limits. I therefore remain for petitioner: no categorical requirement to file a discretionary reconsideration motion, and no sua sponte jurisdictional bar.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest opposing consideration is the functional exhaustion rationale Justice Alito initially emphasized—reconsideration gives the BIA a final chance to correct its own errors—but that policy cannot overcome Congress’s textual limitation to remedies “available … as of right.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas explain, treating a discretionary reconsideration motion (8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a)) as mandatory would collapse “as of right” into a mere right-to-file and effectively add an extra step Congress did not impose. On the jurisdictional label, the clear-statement line Roberts and Justice Kagan cite (Arbaugh, Henderson, Fort Bend, Boechler) confirms § 1252(d)(1) is best treated as a mandatory claims-processing rule, with Union Pacific reinforcing that courts should not convert such prescriptions into power-stripping bars or judicially expand exhaustion beyond the statutory scheme. Practical concerns in immigration’s high-volume system further counsel against reading this provision to require courts to raise forfeiture sua sponte and to force a discretionary, often unavailing motion in every case.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest point—pressed most forcefully as a functional matter—is that reconsideration is the ordinary mechanism for the BIA to correct legal errors before judicial review, so exhaustion’s purposes would be served by requiring it. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, § 1252(d)(1) exhausts only remedies “available … as of right,” and 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a) makes reconsideration discretionary; reading “as of right” to mean merely “permitted to file” collapses the limiting phrase and effectively adds a prerequisite Congress did not impose. On the jurisdictional label, the clear-statement framework Roberts cites (Arbaugh/Henderson/Boechler, echoed by Justice Kagan) and Union Pacific reinforce that we should treat this as a mandatory claims-processing/forfeiture rule rather than a power-stripping jurisdictional bar. Justice Alito’s acknowledgment that the functional appeal cannot override the statutory text confirms that the Fifth Circuit’s categorical requirement of a reconsideration motion is unsustainable on original public meaning grounds.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest opposing point remains Justice Alito’s functional argument that reconsideration best serves exhaustion by letting the BIA correct legal errors first, but text controls: § 1252(d)(1) demands exhaustion only of remedies “available … as of right,” and 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a) makes reconsideration discretionary, so making it mandatory would effectively read the limiting phrase out of the statute. Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s emphasis on the clear-statement rule (Arbaugh/Henderson/Boechler/Fort Bend) reinforces that we should not transform this prerequisite into a jurisdictional bar that courts must police sua sponte, especially in a high-volume system with many unrepresented noncitizens. Union Pacific, as Justice Gorsuch notes, supports keeping the line between mandatory process rules and jurisdiction, and it cautions against judicially elevating discretionary agency mechanisms into categorical gates to review. The government can still invoke forfeiture or issue-exhaustion when properly raised, but it cannot convert discretionary reconsideration into a jurisdictional or categorical prerequisite.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 1252(d)(1) requires exhaustion only of “administrative remedies available to the alien as of right,” and a BIA motion to reconsider is discretionary, so treating failure to file such a motion as a categorical bar goes beyond the statute’s text. Under our clear-statement approach, exhaustion requirements are ordinarily treated as mandatory claims-processing rules—not jurisdictional limits—absent unmistakable jurisdictional language, consistent with Arbaugh, Henderson, and Boechler. Union Pacific reinforces that issue-exhaustion and related exhaustion prescriptions generally “promote the orderly progress of litigation” and do not necessarily “cabin a court’s power,” supporting a nonjurisdictional construction that can be waived or forfeited by the government. A narrow holding that (1) § 1252(d)(1) is nonjurisdictional and (2) does not compel filing a discretionary reconsideration motion best respects precedent and avoids unnecessary disruption in high-volume immigration adjudication.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 8 U.S.C. § 1252(d)(1) requires exhaustion only of remedies “available to the alien as of right,” and a BIA motion to reconsider is discretionary by regulation, see 8 C.F.R. § 1003.2(a), so it is not a remedy available “as of right.” Reading “as of right” to mean merely a right to file would drain the limiting phrase of meaning and effectively mandate reconsideration in every case, atextually expanding the exhaustion obligation beyond what Congress enacted. Separately, under this Court’s clear-statement approach, § 1252(d)(1) lacks the jurisdictional clarity required to strip Article III courts of adjudicatory power, see Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006), so at most it is a mandatory claims-processing rule. The Fifth Circuit therefore erred in treating the failure to seek reconsideration as a jurisdictional bar to review.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 1252(d)(1) bars review unless the noncitizen has exhausted “all administrative remedies available to the alien as of right,” and a motion to reconsider is the ordinary, established mechanism by which the BIA may correct alleged legal error in its own decision—so requiring that step before judicial review sensibly serves exhaustion’s core function of giving the agency the first opportunity to fix mistakes. Even if the Court’s recent cases (e.g., Arbaugh, Henderson, and Boechler) counsel caution in labeling such prerequisites “jurisdictional,” the statute at minimum imposes a mandatory issue-exhaustion requirement that the court of appeals must enforce when properly invoked, and the Fifth Circuit reasonably treated the unraised factfinding challenge as unexhausted. Union Pacific underscores that exhaustion rules are enforced to protect orderly process and to prevent courts from becoming the first forum for claims that should have been presented to the administrative decisionmaker. Given the practical consequences in the immigration context and the government’s strong interest in channeling disputes through the agency, I would affirm the refusal to entertain an issue first raised in court without a motion to reconsider.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 1252(d)(1) requires exhaustion only of “administrative remedies available to the alien as of right,” and a BIA motion to reconsider is discretionary, so it is not an “as of right” remedy that must be pursued to preserve an issue for court review. Under this Court’s clear-statement approach, exhaustion and similar preconditions are ordinarily nonjurisdictional claims-processing rules absent unmistakable jurisdictional language, and § 1252(d)(1) lacks that kind of jurisdictional hook. Treating issue exhaustion here as jurisdictional would also distort adversarial norms and impose severe practical burdens on often-unrepresented or under-resourced noncitizens, contrary to Henderson v. Shinseki’s warning that jurisdictional labels create unfair prejudice and force courts to police issues sua sponte. Union Pacific confirms the distinction between true jurisdictional limits and nonjurisdictional exhaustion requirements, and supports the conclusion that failure to file a discretionary reconsideration motion cannot categorically bar judicial review.

Union Pacific confirms that even when an exhaustion requirement is important, courts should not convert it into a jurisdictional bar without a clear statutory directive, and doing so here would undermine workability in high-volume immigration adjudication by forcing courts to police forfeited issues sua sponte.
